source.title: Neuron to Graph: Interpreting Language Model Neurons at Scale
source.authors: Alex Foote; Neel Nanda; Esben Kran; Ioannis Konstas; Shay B. Cohen; Fazl Barez

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates graph-based neuron representations against held-out neuron activations, a different method for testing whether interpretations predict where neurons fire.
record.gate_note: The quantitative evaluation uses a random half of each neuron's top 20 Neuroscope examples for building a representation and the other half for testing; scores are computed only on tokens that actually fired. Table 1 reports layer-averaged precision, recall and F1 for N2G and two lookup baselines. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results. Case studies and activation trajectories do not directly test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: N2G builds a neuron explanation (a token-context graph) from 10 top-activating examples. It then checks how well that explanation predicts the neuron's firings on 10 held-out top-activating examples. This bears on V6, whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict where neurons fire. It is a different method from inspection or GPT-4 explanation, and the model is one SoLU model.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. N2G captures behaviour well in early layers and only partially in later layers. The authors expect this to worsen in larger models and in non-SoLU Transformers, which have more polysemantic neurons.
record.recipe_differences: N2G builds token-context graphs from maximally activating examples, then evaluates graph predictions; it is not the GPT-4 natural-language explanation method or the Qwen3 pole audit.
record.method_sensitivity: Layer: N2G performance generally declines in deeper layers; 5-gram lookup recall rises with depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Automated graph comparison finds 60 pairs of neurons with near-identical graphs, e.g. one in layer 1 and one in layer 4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Duplicate or redundant neuron features exist across layers. The authors attribute this to superposition or dropout.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix example: one neuron graph has three disconnected subgraphs for phrases in Dutch, English and Swedish, i.e. a polysemantic neuron in a SoLU model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Polysemantic neurons persist even in SoLU models. This is qualitative only, with no rate.

record.problems: Evaluation is limited to one SoLU model and held-out halves of its top 20 activating examples, rather than broad unseen text; only firing tokens are scored. Metrics are averaged across neurons, with no uncertainty estimates, and the paper notes incomplete later-layer coverage.

untested.parts: Shares across other models, MoE, scale.
Architecture/tools causes; vision estimates. SoLU is used as a monosemanticity-promoting architecture, but it is not compared with a non-SoLU model.
Neuron-level attribution graphs without a replacement model.
Natural-language or by-inspection 'one main job' explanations. Prediction on arbitrary text: the test set is held-out top-activating examples only.
Not tested: no fraction of neurons with good scores, no simulation on random new text, no comparison of explainer strength.

record.verdict_notes: Caveats for V6. The 'explanation' is a mechanical graph limited by exact token matching and only 10 training examples. Low scores may reflect N2G's limits rather than neurons lacking a single job; the authors attribute part of the recall drop to incomplete example coverage. Scores are computed only on firing tokens, and no uncertainty is given. Not an original source. The reader's linking to V7 and its labelling of baseline rows were corrected.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole-level shares of single-job, related-job and not-understood neurons.
Shares across model families, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or model scales up to trillions of parameters.
The interpretation of InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization or tools explain late-layer interpretability, and the InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
Whether attribution graphs using a large model's own neurons explain its behaviour without a trained replacement model.

The study tests graph representations built from activating examples, not natural-language explanations; it evaluates a SoLU model on held-out examples from the top-activating set, not arbitrary new text.
It reports layer-averaged predictive metrics, not the fraction of neurons meeting a good-score criterion; it does not compare stronger explainer models.

labels.reason: Table 1: layers 3-5 have F1 0.45/0.38/0.37 and precision 0.45/0.39/0.38. The conclusion says later layers are only partially captured. Explanations fitted to activating examples mispredict many firings.

labels.label: limits_scope
labels.reason: Layers 0-2: F1 0.68/0.65/0.55, recall 0.84/0.82/0.75. The authors say layers 0 and 1 are captured well, so the failure is partial and depends on depth. The authors call layer 2 neither well nor poorly captured.

relation.reason: Its own held-out evaluation of N2G graphs (Table 1) bears on V6.

tranche.reason: Different method (token-context graphs built from top-activating examples, scored on held-out top-activating examples) aimed at whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict firings.

source_check.notes: Test set is the held-out half of each neuron's top-20 Neuroscope examples (threshold 0.5), scored only on firing tokens, so it does not test random or broad text. The text does not say how precision below 1 arises under that scoring. The SoLU model was chosen to minimise polysemanticity. The authors expect more failure in standard Transformers. Author list: Foote, Nanda, Kran, Konstas, Cohen, Barez. Check overlap with 2304.12918 before treating the two as independent.

reader_labels.reason: Held-out predictive scores are imperfect across layers and the authors report that later-layer behaviour is only partially captured; see r01–r18.
